Beauty World Plaza makes fresh collective sale bid at $165 mil
article:
Beauty World Plaza , a 999-year leasehold mixed-use development on Upper Bukit Timah Road , has been launched for collective sale via a public tender exercise, with a guide price of $165 million.

The guide price translates to $2,231 psf of gross floor area, said marketing agent ETC (a member of Realion Group) in an Oct 13 release.

The fresh en bloc bid follows past tender launches for Beauty World Plaza in June 2019 and November 2018. The development was similarly priced at $165 million in both exercises.

Beauty World Plaza is an eight-storey development comprising commercial shops on Levels 1 to 3 and residential apartments on Levels 4 to 8. There is also an open terrace on Level 4.

The development occupies a corner plot along Upper Bukit Timah Road and Bukit Timah Link measuring 24,817 sq ft. The land is zoned for commercial and residential use, with a gross plot ratio of 3.0. It is adjacent to Beauty World MRT Station on the Downtown Line.

The site offers buyers “flexibility to explore different strategies”, said Swee Shou Fern, ETC’s head of investment advisory. “Beyond a conventional redevelopment play, the buyer can also consider asset enhancement for the existing development.”

According to ETC, outline planning permission for serviced apartments has been granted for the site's residential component. The site could yield 108 keys, based on a minimum unit size of 35 sq m (377 sq ft).

“The in-principle planning approval opens up the potential to convert the upper floors to serviced apartments or co-living residences and curate the commercial podium for retail, F&B, lifestyle amenities, enrichment centres or coworking space…subject to authorities’ approval,” Swee commented.

Beauty World Plaza is close to several upcoming developments that are reshaping the Beauty World precinct. These include an integrated transport hub linking Beauty World MRT Station with a new bus interchange, along with The Reserve Residences (an integrated development comprising 732 apartments and retail mall Bukit V) and the 158-unit condo 8@BT .

“Beauty World Plaza is extremely well-placed to benefit from this transformation, given its immediate access to the MRT station and established residential, education and lifestyle catchment,” said Swee.

The development is close to several educational institutions, with Pei Hwa Presbyterian Primary School located within a 1km radius, while Bukit Timah Primary School and Methodist Girsl’ School (Primary) are within a 2km radius.

Within the wider vicinity, tertiary institutions such as the Singapore Institute of Management, Singapore University of Social Sciences and Ngee Ann Polytechnic are a short drive away, along with international schools such as Singapore Korean International School and Chatsworth International School.

The tender will close at 3pm on Nov 19.

title: Vietnam leads Apac branded residences market by number of units, ranks third globally
article:
Vietnam has topped the Asia Pacific (Apac) branded residences market by number of units, with 16,135 residences across 68 completed and pipeline developments.

This makes it the third largest in the world, behind the United Arab Emirates (84,972 units) and the US (71,592 units), according to Global Branded Residences, a UK-based advisory firm that specialises in the market.

The data, compiled in The Brand Standard, the firm’s inaugural annual report, shows that Vietnam has the highest number of branded residential units in Apac despite having fewer developments compared to Thailand, which ranked second. The runner-up has 14,141 branded residences across 73 completed and pipeline projects.

India ranked third for both, with 13,908 residences across 61 developments.

Riyan Itani, founder of Global Branded Residences, notes that while the sector is “usually” measured by the number of developments, looking at the number of units offers further insight. “Counting the residences inside those developments tells you how much product is actually coming to market and how significant the buyer demand actually is.”

In any case, the Apac branded residences market continues to grow, backed by a sizeable pipeline. According to the report, the number of pipeline schemes has surged 36% over the past 12 months, going from 147 projects to 200.

Combined with its 198 completed developments, the region has a total of 398 schemes. It accounts for 20% of global branded residences stock, after North America (452 projects or 23%) and the Middle East and North Africa (Mena) (426 projects or 22%).

Vietnam, Thailand drive growth

Vietnam is currently the biggest contributor to Apac’s pipeline, with 49 projects located across cities such as Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City as well as coastal destinations including Da Nang, Phu Quoc, Hoi An and Ha Long. These include Mercure Residences Ha Long, a 2,259-unit scheme that is the single-largest branded residential development in Apac.

The pipeline is the sixth-largest for a country globally, following the UAE, the US, Mexico, Brazil and Saudi Arabia. Vietnam has completed 19 projects to date.

Thailand is the region’s next-biggest driver, with 37 pipeline developments and 36 completed ones. With 73 projects overall, Thailand is the fifth-biggest market among standalone countries by number of schemes. It is also the third largest for completed stock.

A key market within the country is Phuket, with Global Branded Residences estimating 19 pipeline developments on the Thai island, on top of 13 completed projects. In terms of standalone cities, Phuket is the fifth-largest market in the world by overall developments, behind Dubai, Miami, São Paulo and New York.

All but one of Phuket’s 32 total schemes are in resort locations. This makes it the “largest resort branded residences market in the world”, competing in scale with major capital and gateway cities. “That tells us branded residences are increasingly following international buyers into destinations where lifestyle and leisure are fundamental to the purchasing decision,” adds Itani.

Broader market

The report also highlights that Apac offers a broader spectrum of offerings that reach a wider base in contrast to the North America, Mena and Europe markets. “It has a much wider spread of price points, a strong regional brand ecosystem and an increasingly resort-led pipeline,” says Itani.

Luxury projects account for 61% of Apac’s schemes, compared to 76% for North America. In addition, the region accounts for 54%, 35% and 33% of the midscale, upper-midscale and upscale schemes globally, despite making up less than a quarter of overall stock.

Apac branded residences are also able to command a slightly higher premium versus equivalent non-branded residences. According to the report, Apac schemes have an average price premium of 47%, compared to the global average of 44%.

The premium may reflect the dominance of hotel brands in the region, along with the significance of its resort destinations.

Hotel brands account for 78% of Apac’s overall branded residence schemes, and 82% of pipeline projects. Meanwhile, some 93% of Apac’s resort schemes carry a hotel brand.

Nonetheless, Apac remains the only region worldwide that is not led by Marriott or Accor. The two hospitality giants dominate branded residences elsewhere, making up more than a quarter of overall developments globally.

However, in Apac, Banyan Group leads with around 50 projects, surpassing Accor at 44 and Marriott at 34.

title: Frasers Property appoints ESR's Jai Mirpuri as CEO of industrial and logistics business
article:
Frasers Property has named Jai Mirpuri as the new CEO of Frasers Property Industrial, with effect from Jan 11, 2027. Based in Singapore, Mirpuri will report directly to Frasers Property group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi.

He will replace Reini Otter, who will be stepping down on Dec 17. Otter is leaving to join ESR Group , where he will be CEO of its Australia and New Zealand business. He spent 28 years at Frasers Property, including seven years as CEO of Frasers Property Industrial.

Mirpuri will helm Frasers Property's industrial and logistics operations in Australia and Europe, which includes overseeing the manager of Singapore-listed Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust.

He joins the group from ESR, where he is currently the CEO of ESR Fund Managers and head of Southeast Asia. Before that, he was also the founder and co-CEO of ESR India.

He has been with ESR for over 18 years, having joined in 2008.

“Jai brings deep expertise in the industrial and logistics sector, and a strong track record of building teams and managing platforms,” said Sirivadhanabhakdi in an Oct 13 release. “These credentials, combined with his extensive leadership and customer experience across markets, make him well-placed to drive Frasers Property Industrial’s next phase of growth.”

title: The AI Boom Is Being Built on Debt: Should Investors Be Worried?
article:
Big Tech companies
such as
Meta Platforms
(NASDAQ: META) and
Alphabet
(NASDAQ: GOOGL) were previously known for their cash-rich, fortress balance sheets.
Their financial firepower to fuel the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution was nearly undisputed.
But now, debt is increasingly being used instead to finance data centres, specialised silicon, and the massive grids to power them.
The narrative has shifted from smart AI agents powering the future economy to a grim future of mounting financial debt that could drag down global growth.
Should investors be alarmed?
What Happened to Their Fortress Balance Sheets?
Historically, Big Tech operated as asset-light enterprises.
Their capital expenditure (capex) as a percentage of revenue was reportedly low, in the single digits (about 4%).
Today, the capex at the hyperscalers (the largest cloud-computing providers) amounts to more than half of their revenues.
Collectively, the AI spending by the four hyperscalers – Alphabet,
Amazon
(NASDAQ: AMZN),
Microsoft
(NASDAQ: MSFT), and Meta – is projected to surge 84% in 2026 to US$760 billion.
Crucially, global debt funding towards the AI infrastructural buildout is expected to double, reaching nearly US$570 billion in 2026, and to increase further as the hyperscalers’ capex is tipped to surpass US$1 trillion in 2027.
Related articles:
Microsoft vs Alphabet: Growth, AI and What Investors Need to Know
Amazon and 2 Other Winners: 3 Growth Stocks to Buy Now and Hold for the Long Term
Borrowings and Off-Balance-Sheet Deals
Where is all this capital really coming from?
Corporate bond sales surged 11.8% to US$2.46 trillion in 2025, driven by US hyperscaler-linked issuances.
But the real financial shift lies in off-balance-sheet financing structures.
To preserve their credit ratings, the tech giants are turning to special purpose vehicles (SPVs), private credit, and graphics processing unit (GPU)-backed securitisations.
Consider Meta’s private capital deal with
Blue Owl Capital
(NYSE: OWL), which resulted in the two entities forming an SPV that issued over US$27 billion in private debt backed by Meta’s lease commitment and financial guarantees.
Under this deal, private-credit funds hold 80% of the SPV’s equity while Meta holds the remaining 20% in the Louisiana project.
Importantly, this minority stake allows Meta to keep the associated liabilities off its balance sheet.
Meta is not alone.
Collectively, Big Tech’s off-balance-sheet commitments have reportedly reached US$3.1 trillion, roughly four times greater than their expected capex of US$760 billion in 2026.
Related articles:
Meta Platforms vs OCBC: Which Stock Creates More Value for Shareholders?
If You Invested US$10,000 in Meta at Its IPO, Here’s How Much You’d Have Today
Silicon Obsolescence and Mounting Costs
With such massive leverage, the structural risks are real.
While massive capital to build AI-related hardware is spent upfront at unprecedented speed, the software running on it is monetised much more slowly.
To make matters worse, hardware generally depreciates much faster than software.
Critics have observed that the hyperscalers have artificially stretched the depreciation timelines of their GPUs to aggressively lower expenses and boost their profit margins.
On top of that, the recurring operating expenses of US$2.0 million to US$2.8 million per megawatt per year add pressure to the hyperscalers’ profitability.
A Systemic Bubble?
Rising debt to fund fast-depreciating hardware, without meaningful software revenue to offset it, does not paint a reassuring picture for investors.
Moreover, the true leverage might be understated due to the off-balance-sheet arrangements that obscure the full extent of financial obligations.
Crucially, the risks are interconnected among stakeholders.
Hyperscalers,
neoclouds
(young cloud-computing companies that focus on providing GPUs to customers), private-credit funds, sovereign investors, and even pension funds are linked through contracts and securitised debt, meaning any stress incurred in one of the nodes could send ripples across the whole ecosystem.
A Secular Boom?
Using debt to fund infrastructure is not uncommon, especially for the AI revolution, which is frequently touted as a once-in-a-lifetime industrial revolution.
Despite asset depreciation risks, AI data centres may stay useful for longer than expected, as older computing capacity can be repurposed for less demanding tasks.
What about the risk of a demand shortfall?
Arguably, this is unlikely, given AI’s wide total addressable market that spans across software development, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, research and public services.
What about leveraged players defaulting? That is possible for weaker players.
Therefore, investors should focus on the best-capitalised hyperscalers, which run some of the most profitable, cash-generating business models with healthy margins and strong balance sheets.
They are more likely to survive a shakeout and emerge even stronger.
Get Smart: How Investors Can Navigate the AI Debt Era
The
AI boom
isn’t inherently doomed by debt, but the era of premium valuation multiples is ending as investors demand more visibility for their investments.
Furthermore, given the enormous scale of AI infrastructure, funding it through debt could be considered rational, if done responsibly.
Still, the real risks will surface if spending accelerates with no end in sight while free cash flow dries up and visible returns stall.
For investors, the important question is therefore not “Is AI being built on debt?” but “Can the companies borrowing and investing today generate enough future cash flow to justify that debt?”
Balance-sheet transparency, favourable debt coverage, and monetisation potential should define the winners in the
next phase
of the boom.
Not all AI “winners” will survive this cycle.

title: LVMH’s China slump threatens hopes for wider luxury recovery
article:
(Oct 13): LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE offered a closer look at the deepening Chinese luxury slump this week, revealing that sales on the mainland dropped by double digits in the third quarter while the traditionally high-spending consumer group also pulled back overseas.

The weak spending contributed to a 5% drop in organic revenue in the Asia excluding Japan segment, the only region where the luxury giant saw a year-on-year decline. Chinese shoppers’ purchases overseas declined by a mid-single-digit percentage while overall demand improved later in the quarter ending Sept 30, chief financial officer Cecile Cabanis told analysts on a call.

The China slowdown at LVMH, long seen as an industry bellwether, adds to doubts about the durability of a broader luxury recovery and could offer a worrying signal for rivals, including Yves Saint Laurent owner Kering SA and Hermès International SCA, which are due to report earnings later this month. China had helped fuel an industry rebound less than a year ago but worsening economic sentiment is again weighing on high-end spending.

“The news flow has not been particularly good in China in the summer,” Cabanis said. “So this has really weighed on the feel-good factor and created a short-term subdued Chinese backdrop.”

LVMH shares were little changed in early Paris trading, after declining about 40% this year.

See also: Luxury condos seized in Singapore’s biggest money-laundering case find few buyers

Luxury demand in China is being squeezed on numerous fronts. Consumer wariness amid a broader economic slowdown is restraining spending at home and pushing some shoppers toward cheaper local brands. At the same time, recent stock-market weakness and tougher taxation of overseas wealth are weighing on some of the country’s richest consumers.

“Everybody’s having a tough time,” said Jacques Roizen, co-founder of Shanghai-based consultancy Foresight Performance Partners. “LVMH as a portfolio of scale is such an industry index and the other luxury listed companies are not going to significantly outperform that.”

The slowdown in Chinese demand contrasted with spending by US customers, which rose by a mid-single-digit percentage.

See also: Louis Vuitton loses sales in China after tea logo case backlash

Louis Vuitton also faced public backlash after a trademark dispute with local tea chain Molly Tea stirred criticism in China during the quarter, adding to pressure on LVMH’s biggest label. Cabanis said that while it was difficult to quantify the impact, the consumer pushback hurt Louis Vuitton at least at the beginning of the period.

The setback in China comes as the broader luxury recovery faces pressure from conflict in the Middle East and cost-of-living concerns that are curbing discretionary spending globally.

That pressure is already showing across the luxury sector. Sales at the 25 biggest luxury labels in China dropped more than 10% in July, Bloomberg reported earlier. That threatens to derail a recovery that began less than a year ago, when a stock market boom fuelled by artificial intelligence helped revive luxury spending.

LVMH’s renewed gains in revenue and earnings per share this year “grew precarious” as China’s slowdown deepened in the third quarter, Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Deborah Aitken and Karine Pitton wrote.

“There was a shift in the Chinese consumer backdrop, and this forces us to sharpen our self-help effort,” CFO Cabanis said. “We need to do more but we have not stopped investing in China.”

title: China’s CXMT claims memory breakthrough ahead of Samsung, Hynix
article:
(Oct 13): CXMT Corp declared it achieved a breakthrough in chip technology that rivals like Samsung Electronics Co had pursued for years, an unsubstantiated claim that jolted stocks and reflects China’s aggressive push into a critical sphere.

The domestic memory leader plans to roll out a new type of chip that packs more computing power into a single component, CXMT president Cao Kanyu told an industry conference in Shanghai over the weekend. The upcoming product for data centre servers sports a so-called 4F² design and should launch before the end of the year, Cao said in comments confirmed by a company spokesperson.

If CXMT has succeeded in achieving the 4F² threshold, that means it got there before Samsung and SK Hynix Inc, despite US sanctions that bar the Chinese firm’s access to tools such as ASML Holding NV’s top-end machines. Cao didn’t provide more details, but the widely reported remarks helped spark a sell-off in global chip stocks.

Samsung and SK Hynix shares fell more than 7% in South Korea on Tuesday, weighing down the broader Kospi index, after Micron Technology Inc closed down 4% overnight.

“A successful and earlier implementation of 4F² architecture in DRAM production would vastly improve CXMT’s competitive position versus peers,” said Jing Jie Yu, an analyst with Morningstar. “That said, memory leaders as well as equipment manufacturers have both similarly echoed the difficulty in this technological transition, and we still expect a meaningful time gap between the unveiling of CXMT’s 4F2 product and commercialisation at viable yields.”

Cao’s declaration — months after CXMT briefly became China’s most valuable company following a blockbuster summer IPO — underscores its effort to close the gap with foreign rivals in chipmaking, an area essential to AI development.

See also: Chip sell-off triggers 7% Korea rout after CEO’s ‘casino’ warning

The industry’s existing 6F² standard refers to a surface area of 6-times the square of the “feature size” of a chip: the basic line-width between transistors. Samsung and SK Hynix are exploring ways to shrink that to 4F², in theory packing the same cells into a smaller area for greater efficiency.

CXMT’s Cao said it’s changing the way transistors are laid out via stacking. The so-called Vertical Surrounding Gate approach should reduce leakage and other side effects — a problem long associated with efforts by bigger rivals to reduce sizes beyond the 6F² standard.

If it works, the new architecture marks the latest example of innovative workarounds that Chinese companies from Huawei Technologies Co to DeepSeek devise to get around US technology curbs.

See also: Microsoft bets on homegrown Maia AI chip to challenge Nvidia

“Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks,” said Vey-Sern Ling, a managing director at Union Bancaire Privee.

Huawei in May unveiled its Tau Scaling Law, an alternative to the decades-old Moore’s Law of shrinking transistors to boost chip performance. The Chinese chip champion instead seeks to speed up transmission and increase transistor density within a chip through LogicFolding. It’s already rolled out chips using this technology that run on smartphones launched this year.

CXMT is racing to ramp up production of advanced memory to meet surging AI demand. The ability to manufacture sophisticated products would also position the company better as a global supply crunch begins to ease in coming years.

It remains a laggard in high-bandwidth memory, the type of semiconductors used in Nvidia Corp AI accelerators. Still, it’s making steady progress in the broader DRAM market. The company’s share of that field had expanded to 10% by the second quarter of this year, compared to just 4% a year ago, data compiled by Counterpoint Research shows.

title: Hong Kong lifeline buys Cheng family time to save New World
article:
(Oct 13): It was a Wednesday evening in late September and analysts covering New World Development Co were getting antsy. The cash-strapped Hong Kong developer was late to report its earnings and executives had not shown up to a scheduled briefing.

Behind the scenes, New World was scrambling to hammer out a deal that, when announced hours later, would give it a crucial lifeline, according to people familiar with the matter. Hong Kong’s Airport Authority agreed to waive billions of dollars in rent the company had committed to pay for its struggling 11 Skies project near the airport, alleviating its debt burden.

In return, the Airport Authority would fully take over the HK$18 billion mega mall-and-office complex — and get an option to buy a significant chunk of the developer’s shares at a steep discount. The agreement came with a key condition: the founding Cheng family must remain New World’s largest shareholder.

The unusual deal shows how far Hong Kong authorities are prepared to go to stabilise one of the city’s biggest property developers as New World faces nearly US$11 billion of debt coming due as early as next year. It buys the billionaire Cheng family more time to shore up a company that posted a record US$3.6 billion loss in its recent fiscal year.

New World will also give HK$3 billion in cash and services to the Airport Authority as part of the agreement.

The pseudo-bailout sends a clear message: the city’s property tycoons, who have built Hong Kong into what it is today but are also responsible for sustaining one of the world’s most expensive and inequitable property markets, are too big to fail.

See also: Six-storey commercial building at Middle Road for sale at $80 mil

“The deal highlights New World’s economic and policy relevance to Hong Kong, particularly as the government pushes ahead” with an ambitious plan to develop a new area in the northern part of the city that needs support from developers, said Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis. “Further financial pressure on New World could increase restructuring or default risks.”

Representatives for New World and the Cheng family did not respond to requests for comment. The Airport Authority declined to comment beyond its earlier announcement on the 11 Skies agreement, which said the project paves the way for further development of the airport area.

New World shares were flat in Hong Kong trading Tuesday afternoon. The stock has fallen nearly 29% this year, compared with a 5.4% drop in the benchmark Hang Seng Index.

See also: 999-year strata-titled shophouse in Binjai Park for sale at $4.4 mil

The 11 Skies agreement also gives the Chengs breathing room to act on New World’s capital structure — until late 2029. As part of the deal, the Airport Authority can buy 750 million New World shares — about a 30% stake — from the family’s investment arm Chow Tai Fook Enterprises Ltd within three years for HK$2.25 billion, which amounts to about a roughly 43% discount to the developer’s current share price.

But since the option is conditional on Chow Tai Fook remaining New World’s largest shareholder, the Cheng family will need to inject fresh capital or expand New World’s equity base before the Airport Authority can exercise its right.

The 11 Skies exit represents “a great leap toward equity raising” and may implicitly signal an equity deal within three years, UBS Group AG analysts including Mark Leung wrote this month.

Investors hope that the deal will inject momentum into talks between the Chengs and a variety of co-investment partners that have dragged on for more than a year, amid the family’s reluctance to cede power.

Most recently, the Chengs discussed a potential investment with Bain Capital, separate people familiar with the matter said. But macroeconomic uncertainty has made both the investor and the family more cautious about a deal.

Discussions with Blackstone Inc over a US$4 billion tie-up ended earlier this year after the Cheng family refused to give up control of the company, people familiar said in May.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The overlap between New World’s fortunes and the Hong Kong government’s ambitions has deep roots. During the city’s property downturn in the 1980s, New World pressed ahead with major investments — like the landmark Convention and Exhibition Centre — to help boost confidence. The Chengs have also been enthusiastic investors in mainland China, including on infrastructure and urban redevelopment projects.

Local regulators have also taken an interest in New World’s stability. When the developer was trying to refinance a record amount of debt last year, Hong Kong Monetary Authority officials contacted lenders directly before a rollover agreement was reached days before the deadline.

The economic backdrop has become less favourable in the past year. China’s efforts to claw back tax revenue from wealthy citizens’ overseas assets and higher interest rates in Hong Kong could threaten the city’s nascent property recovery, which had been one of the few tailwinds for New World.

In the meantime, the Chengs are leaning on other liquidity measures, including debt swaps and extending loan maturities. New World has announced an exchange offer for about US$991 million in bonds due in 2027 and 2028, following a previous 3.24 billion yuan asset spin-off in Shanghai.

“The Cheng family has been working assiduously to repair New World’s finances but has yet to put any of its additional private capital at risk,” said Brock Silvers, managing director at private equity firm Kaiyuan Capital. “That may soon change.”

title: Copper and aluminium drop as AI selloff saps appetite for risk
article:
(Oct 13): Copper and aluminium retreated as investor angst around overheated spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure fuelled uncertainty about the demand outlook for the metals.

AI and technology stocks dropped across global markets following warnings the rapid buildout of data centres will become more difficult to finance. South Korea’s equity benchmark — which has been correlated with copper prices at times this year — slumped as much as 7%.

Copper bulls argue that AI infrastructure will be a key source of demand in the coming decade and any doubts about the pace of spending can hit trading sentiment. Still, the major driver for the red metal’s 17% rally this year has been the threat of US import tariffs, which has pulled huge volumes into the country and cut availability elsewhere.

“While not acting as the sole rationale behind the copper price performance in 2026 thus far, AI-driven sentiment is expected to continue to shape, if not dominate, the narrative in the coming years,” BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said in a note.

Copper fell 0.2% to US$14,588 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 11.25am in Shanghai. Aluminium, which is also used in AI infrastructure, dropped 0.3% and zinc lost 0.7%. Iron ore declined 0.3% to US$90.70 a tonne in Singapore, touching the lowest level in two years.

title: India’s rupee gains most in Asia as RBI widens currency curbs
article:
(Oct 13): India’s rupee extended gains as the central bank widened currency curbs to support the rupee, which faces pressure from high oil prices and foreign outflows.

The rupee outperformed Asian peers Tuesday, rising as much as 0.8% to 95.01 per dollar, following Monday’s 1% gain, as the Reserve Bank of India extended curbs on certain types of derivative transactions to avoid pressuring the currency.

“The negative bias for the rupee has turned, at least for now,” said Dilip Parmar, currency analyst at HDFC Securities. The accelerated strength in the currency is being driven by an unwinding of positions that were earlier exerting strain on the rupee, with liquidity also thinner, he said.

The range for now is 95.10-96 per dollar, he said, adding that a break on the stronger side could take the currency to 94.50.

The central bank backed up its regulatory measures with currency-market interventions that further boosted the rupee’s gains on Tuesday, according to traders familiar with the developments. The currency is still down more than 5% this year, ranking as one of Asia’s weaker performers.

See also: Goldman says markets underestimating how far yuan can rise

The series of regulatory interventions over the past few days highlight the RBI’s resolve to rein in the rupee’s weakness after its first interest-rate increase in nearly four years did little to alter the currency’s course. It also shows that elevated oil prices and persistent foreign outflows from local stocks are keeping policymakers on guard against further depreciation.

Late Monday, the RBI said that banks with operating units in the International Financial Services Centre can only offer offshore rupee-linked derivatives to non-residents for the purpose of hedging. It also widened the scope of a newly-introduced foreign-exchange risk reserve, making it applicable for banks’ own assets and liabilities.

The moves add to steps taken over the weekend, including a special window for oil firms’ dollar demand and broad restrictions on derivatives markets. These represent the strongest rupee-defence measures taken by the RBI since the 2013 taper tantrum episode, with the currency marking several fresh lows over the past year.

See also: South Korean won hits two-year high on lower oil, dollar sales

“Currency-market arbitrage has anyway been pretty much neutralised and the fresh restrictions are another step in that direction,” said Kunal Sodhani, head of treasury at Shinhan Bank in Mumbai, referring to transactions where traders profit from price differences in the onshore and offshore markets.

“These measures are primarily designed to manage market behaviour and volatility,” he said.

Still, there are some who forecast further weakness for the rupee. The currency will gradually weaken to 97.50 per dollar by the September quarter next year, Michael Wan, senior currency analyst at MUFG Bank in Singapore, wrote in a note.

title: Crypto wallet tampering fallout widens as OneKey drops Malaysian reseller
article:
(Oct 13): Crypto hardware maker OneKey has revoked CryptoBilis’s authorisation as a reseller of its products, widening the fallout from the discovery that some Ledger wallets sold through the Malaysian retailer had funds stolen.

“We have no reports of OneKey users losing assets in this incident but we are acting as if the risk is real,” Hong Kong-based OneKey said in a statement on its website. “CryptoBilis is no longer an authorised OneKey reseller.”

Paris-based Ledger SAS said it is investigating reports that users lost funds after buying its hardware wallets through CryptoBilis. The on-chain research group YFarmX estimates that as much as US$103 million was stolen. Ledger has not confirmed the amount lost but said it verified that one affected user’s device contained an unauthorised hardware implant.

The incident is the latest in a series of attacks to plague the crypto industry in recent months, including the theft of more than US$100 million in bitcoin from Coldcard-branded wallets made by Canada-based Coinkite Inc. Hardware wallets, commonly used for cold storage, are considered among the more secure methods of holding cryptocurrency because they use physical devices to store private keys offline.

CryptoBilis said on Oct 10 it had paused the sale and shipment of all hardware wallets across its stores and online channels in Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia.

“We are doing this as a precaution, to protect our customers while Ledger’s investigation continues and while we review our own processes with the help of independent specialists,” it said in a post on X.

See also: Singapore Bitcoin investors seek more returns but prioritise control

Following the reports, CryptoBilis co-founder Arravind Prabu posted on LinkedIn that the reseller was acquired earlier this year and that management responsibilities were handed over in March. CryptoBilis didn’t immediately respond to an emailed request for comment.

Ledger said the number of impacted devices is limited and it is working with relevant authorities.

“We know this is concerning, especially for those directly affected and we are reaching out to impacted users,” it said in a post on X. All confirmed cases related to the incident involve devices sold through CryptoBilis, it added.

See also: Bitcoin falls as US$600 mil in risky crypto bets wiped out

OneKey said devices bought from CryptoBilis between March 1 and Oct 12 can be replaced for free. It has also stopped onboarding new resellers and will review existing ones, it said.

OneKey, a rival to hardware-wallet makers Ledger and Trezor, is backed by Coinbase Ventures and YZi Labs, the family office of Binance Holdings co-founders Changpeng Zhao and Yi He.

title: Visa approved to prepare domestic payments business in China
article:
(Oct 13): Visa Inc received approval to begin preparations to establish a domestic bank card clearing business in China, as the firm follows rivals Mastercard Inc and American Express Co in serving the country’s massive payments market.

“We greatly appreciate the important role of the leaders of the United States and China in pursuing a constructive and strategically stable relationship between the world’s largest economies,” Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said in the statement.

The company’s Beijing unit won the green light from the People’s Bank of China, the official Xinhua News Agency reported Tuesday. It must complete preparatory work within one year before applying to commence operations and obtaining the clearing business licence, Xinhua added.

Visa’s clearance of the regulatory hurdle will allow it to operate in China’s US$144 trillion payments market and mark the end of its years-long pursuit. Visa applied for the licence in 2017, local media reported. Competitor Mastercard received approval to establish its bank card clearing business in 2020 and Amex’s joint venture in the country was approved to start bank card clearing services several months after that.

For years, the battle for entry into mainland China’s massive domestic clearing market was a primary friction point in the broader trade dispute between the world’s two largest economies.

Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump said he brought up Visa’s request for access to mainland China’s market during a meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing. Visa’s CEO McInerney accompanied Trump on that May trip to China. Xi later met his counterpart in Washington in late September, with both agreeing on a trade truce extension. The two are scheduled to talk again in person on the sidelines of the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November.

See also: China passenger vehicle retail sales drop 24% in September

China first signalled an opening in the sector in June 2015, announcing that foreign bank card clearing providers could apply for licenses by establishing local units or through acquisitions. The move was designed to dismantle the long-standing monopoly held by state-run China UnionPay Co.

While the approval marks a significant milestone, Visa is entering a market that looks very different from the one it first sought to enter. China’s payments ecosystem is now dominated by domestic mobile platforms Alipay and WeChat Pay, which have largely bypassed traditional card networks and become the primary channels for everyday transactions.

China had 10.2 billion bank cards in circulation at the end of 2025, with transaction value totalling 963.6 trillion yuan last year, according to the People’s Bank of China.

title: World economy holds up but nears limits of resilience, IMF says
article:
(Oct 13): The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said global growth should pick up next year with a boost from AI investment, but warned the world economy is nearing the limits of its resilience as the energy squeeze persists and financial risks build.

Growth will accelerate to 3.4% in 2027, the fund said Tuesday in its World Economic Outlook. That’s unchanged from the last update in July, while the forecast for this year was raised slightly to 3.1%.

Businesses “have continued to adjust to repeated shocks” while markets — buoyed by an exuberant tech industry — have taken a “broadly benign view of the challenges,” the IMF said.

But it also outlined several reasons why that may not last.

The world has run down its energy inventories to absorb supply shortages since the US attacked Iran, and those buffers could wear thin as the conflict drags on. The artificial intelligence boom has powered demand for hardware and could deliver broad gains in productivity, but it comes with financial risks attached. And the recent surge in bond yields makes it urgent to trim budget deficits and public debts.

See also: HSBC moves to Wall Street bonus model, cuts fixed-pay deals

“The global economy has been resilient but that resilience its reaching its limits” and risks to growth are tilted to the downside, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said.

Even with next year’s expected rebound, global growth would be lagging the 3.5% average over the previous two years, and the fund described medium-term prospects as “lackluster.”

See also: Healey needs £35 bil to meet UK spending plans, institute says

One reason is that the boost from AI is so uneven, and the report highlights gaps that are opening up as the technology advances. Almost two-thirds of the extra trade in computing hardware is sourced from just two countries, Taiwan and South Korea, according to the IMF. Meanwhile the US and China accounted for more than 75% of net AI-related imports last year.

The result is that global economic growth rests on a narrower base. Only 32 economies now account for 95% of the overall expansion, the IMF said, compared with 54 countries six months ago.

Whether the surge in AI-related demand “will transform into a positive supply shock in the long term by delivering faster productivity growth remains to be seen,” the IMF said. Meanwhile it’s “contributing to inflationary pressures and financial fragility.”

Still, the fund expects inflation to slow down next year. It forecasts that the global headline rate will fall back to 4.1% — where it was in 2025 — after spiking to 4.7% this year.

As for the budget challenges highlighted by the bond-market slump, the IMF said there’s an urgent need for “credible adjustment plans” to restore fiscal buffers.

“The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding,” Tenreyro said.

The expected pickup in growth next year hinges on an acceleration in emerging and developed economies. In the advanced ones, the IMF sees the expansion slowing to 1.8%, from 2.1% this year.

It predicts growth of 2.3% in the US, the world’s biggest economy — a slight upgrade to the 2.2% forecast in July. For China the 2027 forecast is unchanged at 4%.

Among major economies, the hit to France stands out. Its economy is set to expand only 0.4% this year and 0.7% in 2027. Both figures are 0.2 percentage point lower than in the fund’s July forecasts.

Germany is expected to grow 1.1% in 2027, while growth in the UK will edge down to 1.2% as energy prices and high interest rates weigh on consumption.
